title: Why Do Numerical Solvers Allocate? Zero-Allocation Symplectic Integrators in Rust vs C PETSc
target_audience: Systems programmers, scientific computing engineers, numerical simulation developers
post_body:
Why do standard numerical solvers trigger heap allocations in the inner step loop, and how can we eliminate this memory bottleneck in Rust?

When integrating long-horizon Hamiltonian systems and stiff ODEs in Rust, eliminating dynamic heap allocations in the inner Newton-Krylov solver is essential to avoid memory bandwidth saturation and cache thrashing.

### Architectural Constraints & Solutions
1. Static Workspace Structure: Pass a contiguous `&mut [f64]` buffer slice into the integrator. All stage intermediates, Runge-Kutta vectors, and Krylov directions are mapped onto sub-slices with zero runtime allocations.
2. In-Place CSR Sparse Pattern Reuse: Perform the sparsity symbolic analysis once during initialization. In subsequent Newton steps, update the Jacobian values slice in-place without touching index buffers.
3. Symplectic Conservation: Enforcing symplectic phase-space volume preservation bounds Hamiltonian energy drift to |Delta H / H_0| < 1e-4 over millions of integration steps.

### Boundary Limitations
The zero-allocation guarantee strictly applies to fixed-dimensional phase spaces. Non-periodic or adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) requires bounded buffer pooling.
